meta.title: Polish C1
meta.subtitle: 1,200 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Polish → English (see the Polish, recall the meaning) and English → Polish (see an English meaning, recall the Polish). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1,200 words for level C1 of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Poland's State Commission for the Certification of Proficiency in Polish as a Foreign Language examines at all six levels, but no official word list was found for any of them. So 968 of the 1,200 words were written for Folio, a topic at a time, for the topics the C1 exam is described as covering — extreme sports, the housing market and household repairs, the modern workplace, education and its history, genetically modified food, auctions, the health-care system and insurance, natural disasters, corruption and money laundering, the army and international relations, science and ethics, the Church, the regions and Polish history, and the official, scientific and journalistic styles — together with the vocabulary of the economy, the law, politics, the media, the mind, literature and philosophy, the words of irony, rhetoric and argument, and the forms the level's grammar names (habitual verbs, augmentatives, collective numerals, compounds). They are Folio's choice, not the Commission's, and this is not an official word list. No word taught in the levels below is repeated. The other 232 are the commonest words of everyday Polish not already chosen, from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles, each word counted over all its forms. The cards are ordered by that frequency, so the words met most often come first; the 48 set phrases, which a list of single words cannot count, come last. Polish changes the endings of its nouns, adjectives and verbs, and many stems change with them, so each card carries the forms that cannot be guessed, read from a dictionary rather than generated. 684 nouns show their gender, three cases of the singular and two of the plural. 270 verbs show their aspect and its partner, the forms for ja (I), on (he) and oni (they) and the past of on — a perfective verb's being its future, since it has no present. 31 adjectives show their comparative and superlative. Real example sentences come with 688 of the 1,200 words, three apiece for 402, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Meanings, forms and parts of speech: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency ordering: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
